findings.headline: The council's wholly-owned housing company, Barley Homes Group Limited, received an unqualified audit opinion for 2024-2025.
findings.detail: External auditors reviewed Barley Homes (Group) Limited for 2024-2025 and found its financial statements compliant with Companies Act requirements. This stands in contrast to the qualified opinion on the parent council's accounts, indicating that the governance and accounting controls within the subsidiary are adequate.
findings.matters: The council's ability to use its housing company for housing delivery and economic development depends on sound controls and clean audit opinions. An unqualified opinion provides assurance that the subsidiary can function as intended despite audit issues in the parent council.
findings.quote: The audit found that the Company's financial statement provided a true and fair view of its affairs and was in accordance with the requirements of the Companies Act 2006.

findings.headline: Government has withdrawn the decision to create three unitary authorities in Suffolk, removing a major structural change the council was planning for.
findings.detail: On 7 September 2026, the Secretary of State announced a review of local government reorganisation and withdrew the March 2026 decision that the council had been preparing for. The council had submitted a joint proposal with other Suffolk councils in September 2025 based on the then-stated government commitment to create three unitary authorities. While the government has re-stated commitment to future structural simplification, the timing and form are now uncertain.
findings.matters: Reorganisation would have had major implications for the council's funding, structure, and viability. Its withdrawal removes a defined planning assumption but leaves uncertainty about whether and when future restructuring might occur, affecting the council's strategic outlook and medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 7 September 2026, March 2026, September 2025
findings.quote: government has withdrawn its decision made in March 2026 to create three new unitary authorities in Suffolk

findings.headline: The 2024-2025 accounts carry a qualified audit opinion due to unresolved issues from two years prior.
findings.detail: External auditors signed off the 2024-2025 accounts on 21 January 2026, ahead of the 27 February backstop date. However, a qualified opinion was issued rather than an unqualified one, because the 2022-2023 accounts had received a disclaimer of opinion (the most severe audit classification). This left insufficient audit evidence for the opening balances used in 2024-2025, preventing the auditors from verifying the current year's position against prior years.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion weakens lender confidence in the accuracy of the council's financial statements. The underlying cause — a prior-year disclaimer of opinion — indicates unresolved governance or financial reporting control issues.
findings.figures: 21 January 2026, 27 February 2026
findings.quote: due to the disclaimer of opinion on the 2022 to 2023 accounts and the resultant lack of audit evidence for the opening balances for 2024 to 2025 a qualified opinion for the 2024 to 2025 accounts was issued.

findings.headline: Council assessed as going concern with sufficient liquidity for next 12 months and forecast cash balances of £10m at March 2027.
findings.detail: The council confirmed going concern status based on: (a) robust current and forecast financial position; (b) balanced budgets set for 2026-27 and 2027-28; (c) £6.13m General Fund and £52.01m earmarked reserves; (d) cash flow modelling showing ability to work within Capital Financing Requirement without operational borrowing; (e) access to £29.5m cash and short-term investments; (f) forecast £10m cash at March 2027.
findings.matters: Going concern is foundational to all lending decisions. The council's formal assessment, with detailed supporting evidence on cash, reserves and budgeting, provides assurance on financial continuity.
findings.figures: £29.5m cash and investments at 31 March 2026; £10m forecast cash at March 2027; £6.13m General Fund; £52.01m earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Overall, based on its cash flow forecast, borrowing potential and access to investment funds, as well as the level of general fund and reserve balances it holds, the council determines that it has sufficient liquidity to continue to deliver services for the foreseeable future.

findings.headline: Government withdrew March 2026 decision to create three unitary authorities in Suffolk, creating strategic uncertainty.
findings.detail: On 7 September 2026, the Secretary of State announced withdrawal of the March 2026 decision to create three new unitary authorities in Suffolk following 'updated and privileged legal advice'. The government restated commitment to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying council structures. West Suffolk states it 'remains a high performing and ambitious council' and 'remains financially sound' despite this structural uncertainty.
findings.matters: Unitary authority creation would have triggered significant transition costs and restructuring. Withdrawal removes that immediate risk but creates uncertainty about future structure. Lenders need to know this is a managed strategic uncertainty, not a financial crisis.
findings.figures: Decision withdrawn 7 September 2026 (9 days before committee meeting date)
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026, the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government announced that she would be reviewing the current plans for local government reorganisation in Suffolk, as well as other areas of the country, following 'updated and privileged legal advice'. As such, government has withdrawn its decision made in March 2026 to create three new unitary authorities in Suffolk.

findings.headline: External borrowing £9m against £122.1m authorised boundary, indicating significant undrawn borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: The council held only £9m external borrowing at 31 March 2026 while authorized to borrow up to £122.1m for capital programme support, primarily from PWLB or National Wealth Fund. This represents 7.4% of authorized headroom utilised, leaving £113.1m undrawn capacity.
findings.matters: Borrowing headroom is crucial for capital flexibility. Low draw-down against authorization shows the council is not over-leveraged and can access funds for future capital needs if required.
findings.figures: £9m external borrowing; £122.1m authorised boundary; £113.1m undrawn capacity
findings.quote: The council held external borrowing totalling £9 million at 31 March 2026, against an authorised boundary for borrowing for capital programme support of £122.1 million, as set out in our prudential indicators (intended to be sourced primarily from the Public Works Loan Board or the National Wealth Fund).

findings.headline: Pension fund shows underlying net asset of £93.43m, though asset ceiling restricts reported position to £1.075m liability.
findings.detail: The actuarial valuation at 31 March 2026 showed the pension fund's assets exceeded liabilities, with the council's proportion valued at £93.43m net asset. However, IAS 19 asset ceiling rules restrict the recognized asset to zero and create a reported liability of £1.075m. The council notes 'the underlying net defined benefit asset of £93.43 million shows that the council's pension fund is currently in a healthy position, being able to meet its underlying commitments in the long run'.
findings.matters: Unfunded pension liabilities are a major drain on council finances. The underlying asset position, though restricted in financial reporting, indicates the fund can meet long-term benefit commitments without urgent employer cash calls.
findings.figures: Net asset £93.43m; reported liability £1.075m (asset ceiling impact £94.505m); fund actuarial gain from favourable financial assumptions
findings.quote: the underlying net defined benefit asset of £93.43 million shows that the council's pension fund is currently in a healthy position, being able to meet its underlying commitments in the long run to pay retirement benefits.

findings.headline: Capital programme of £27.7m delivered across priority investments including housing, waste and decarbonisation.
findings.detail: The council spent £27.7m on capital including £1.2m for Better Recycling, £3.3m for waste management station land, £2.2m on temporary accommodation properties, £2.3m on Bury Leisure Centre, £2.1m on decarbonisation, £3.1m loaned to housing company Barley Homes, and £3.2m on property and leisure asset management. Funded from reserves (£7.1m), grants (£5.3m), capital receipts (£6.1m) and borrowing.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council can execute strategic capital programmes and diversify revenue through reinvestment. Housing and leisure investments particularly matter for social outcomes and council tax base stability.
findings.figures: £27.7m total; £1.2m recycling; £3.3m waste land; £2.2m housing; £2.3m leisure; £2.1m decarbonisation; £3.1m housing company; £3.2m asset management
findings.quote: The council's capital expenditure for 2025 to 2026 (set out in the same report as in 5.4 above) totalled around £27.7 million, which included investment in preparing for the commencement of the national Better Recycling initiatives (£1.2 million), the purchase of land for the potential extension of the municipal waste management station (£3.3 million).

findings.headline: Housing-related income recovered strongly in 2025-26 after significant shortfall in prior year.
findings.detail: After suffering a significant income shortfall in 2024-25, the council saw a 'good bounce-back' in planning, building control and land charges income in 2025-26. Additional income strength came from solar farm, car-park usage and Apex venue ticket sales. Some income shortfalls remained from vacancies in the property estate.
findings.matters: Income volatility is a key risk for councils and a concern for lenders. This recovery shows the shortfall was cyclical, not structural. Housing market income is typically tied to economic conditions and loan servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Not specified separately, but housing market income bounce-back contributed to overall position 'close to plan'
findings.quote: This is supported by above budget performance in income from our solar farm, car-park usage and ticket sales at the Apex venue in Bury St Edmunds. There are some shortfalls caused by reduced utility and service level income from vacancies in West Suffolk Council's property estate.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve grew to £6.13m, exceeding £5m minimum policy level by £1.27m.
findings.detail: The General Fund increased from £5.625m to £6.13m during the year. After committing £0.83m to the High Street Competitiveness Fund in the 2026-27 budget, an uncommitted balance of £5.27m remains, which exceeds the council's £5m minimum policy. The council also identified £8.8m of earmarked reserves available immediately for unforeseen events.
findings.matters: Healthy reserve cover is essential protection for creditors. A lender needs confidence the council can absorb budget shocks without cutting service debt payments.
findings.figures: General Fund £6.13m at 31 March 2026 (up from £5.625m); uncommitted balance £5.27m; immediately available earmarked reserves £8.8m
findings.quote: This grew to a balance of £6.13 million at 31 March 2026. £0.83 million of this balance will be partly utilised to meet the funding requirements of the High Street Competitiveness Fund included in the 2026 to 2027 Budget. This is in excess of the agreed £5 million policy level.

findings.headline: Council delivered £505,702 surplus after managing variances across income and expenditure.
findings.detail: The year ended with a surplus of £505,702 representing 0.70% of total income budget. This came despite global economic pressures on inflation, energy costs and utility spending, which were offset by higher investment income from interest rates and fuel price savings.
findings.matters: Demonstrates financial discipline and ability to live within budget. Surplus councils have better prospects for servicing debt and absorbing future shocks.
findings.figures: £505,702 surplus (0.70% of £73m budget)
findings.quote: the year-end position included a number of variances to budget, with the overall outturn showing a surplus position of £505,702 (0.70 per cent of the total income budget).

findings.headline: Pension fund valuation results in £1.075 million balance sheet liability after asset ceiling adjustment, though contribution rates are determined separately
findings.detail: The IAS19 pension valuation shows fund assets exceeded liabilities by £93.430 million. International Accounting Standards require an asset ceiling adjustment of £94.505 million, resulting in a £1.075 million pension liability on the balance sheet. The council clarifies that pension contribution rates are determined by a separate triennial actuarial review, not by this accounting valuation.
findings.matters: The pension liability appears on the council's balance sheet and affects net asset position; lenders need to understand whether the liability represents a real cash obligation or an accounting treatment
findings.figures: Fund assets exceeded liabilities by £93.430 million; asset ceiling adjustment of £94.505 million; resulting balance sheet liability of £1.075 million
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026 the effect of the council's asset ceiling has been to reduce the net asset position by £94.505 million, resulting in a liability of £1.075 million that is shown in the balance sheet.

findings.headline: Revenue outturn delivered a £0.506 million surplus, avoiding overspending and increasing the general fund reserve to £6.13 million
findings.detail: The council's in-year revenue expenditure remained within budget, delivering a surplus. This demonstrates effective financial control despite significant capital investment activity during the year.
findings.matters: Revenue surplus indicates financial discipline and absence of service overspending; lenders treat this as evidence of sound budget management
findings.figures: Revenue surplus of £0.506 million; general fund reserve stands at £6.13 million as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: the council's revenue outturn showed a surplus of £0.506 million, resulting in an increase in its general fund reserve, which stands at £6.13 million as at 31 March 2026

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell by 7.4%, from £71.9 million to £66.6 million, as capital projects were funded from revenue reserves
findings.detail: The council used £7.1 million from revenue reserves to fund capital expenditure during 2025-26. Total usable reserves decreased by £5.3 million across the year. Capital investment included recycling facilities, waste management land purchase, temporary accommodation, and leisure centre refurbishment.
findings.matters: Reserves are a critical financial buffer for councils; lenders examine reserve balances carefully as a measure of financial resilience and capacity to weather pressures
findings.figures: Usable reserves decreased from £71.9 million to £66.6 million (net decrease of £5.3 million); £7.1 million of £27.7 million capital spend funded from revenue reserves
findings.quote: During 2025 to 2026 the total value of the council's usable reserves decreased from £71.9 million (at 1 April 2025) to £66.6 million (at 31 March 2026), a net decrease of £5.3 million.

findings.headline: Audit opinion remains provisional with multiple procedures outstanding: pensions valuation, group accounts, and rebuild assurance work not yet complete.
findings.detail: EY states that several items remain outstanding including receipt of finalised financial statements, completion of subsequent events procedures, pensions valuation work, group accounts reconciliation, and rebuild of assurance procedures on assets last valued in 2022/23 and reserves. Until all procedures are complete, the final form of the audit opinion cannot be confirmed and new issues may emerge.
findings.matters: A provisional opinion means the audit is not yet concluded and there remains the possibility that additional issues could emerge that change the opinion or add new qualifications. This extends uncertainty about the final audit outcome and timing of financial statement sign-off.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Given that the audit process is still ongoing, we will continue to challenge the remaining evidence provided and the final disclosures in the Annual Report and Accounts which could influence our final audit opinion.

findings.headline: Scale fee variations proposed for 2025/26 audit to cover recovery programme work, pensions specialists, and new system implementation.
findings.detail: The base scale fee for 2025/26 is £222,242 (versus £216,190 in 2024/25). A 2024/25 scale fee variation of £21,812 has been approved. A further variation for 2025/26 is proposed (amount TBD) to cover work including EY pensions specialists, new FAR system implementation, rebuild of assurance over disclaimed-period balances, and qualified opinion reporting procedures.
findings.matters: Audit cost increases indicate sustained effort required to rebuild assurance from the 2023/24 disclaimer. Higher audit costs represent additional financial burden on the council and indicate ongoing remediation and assurance-building needs that extend beyond routine audit.
findings.figures: Base scale fee £222,242; 2024/25 variation approved £21,812; 2025/26 variation TBD
findings.quote: We propose to submit a scale fee variation to PSAA for additional 2025/26 work covering the following areas: Work of EY Pensions specialists, including additional considerations arising from the 2025 actuarial valuation; Work performed on implementation of new system (FAR); Buildback costs in obtaining assurances over balances subject to backstop disclaimers

findings.headline: No value for money concerns: auditor completed detailed work and identified no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, or efficiency arrangements.
findings.detail: EY completed detailed Value for Money risk assessment and audit procedures with no risks of significant weaknesses identified in the council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of its resources.
findings.matters: VFM assessment covers whether the council is using its resources effectively to deliver services. No issues suggests the council's governance and service delivery arrangements are not under audit scrutiny, reducing risk to service continuity.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We have completed our detailed VFM work and identified no risks of significant weaknesses in arrangements and therefore expect to have no matters to report by exception in our audit opinion.

findings.headline: No significant internal control deficiencies identified, despite recovery from prior audit issues.
findings.detail: Despite the 2023/24 disclaimed opinion and ongoing recovery programme, EY's audit procedures did not identify any significant deficiencies in the council's internal control environment. The auditor adopted a fully substantive approach to audit testing.
findings.matters: Significant control weaknesses would limit confidence in financial reporting and require lenders to place less reliance on management's assertions. The absence of control deficiencies, despite prior audit issues, provides assurance that remediation has been effective.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: During the audit, we did not identify any significant deficiencies in internal control. We have taken a wholly substantive approach to the audit.

findings.headline: Unit4 Asset Module fixed asset register system successfully implemented in March 2026 with no audit issues identified in data transfer.
findings.detail: The council replaced its manual asset register (Asset 400) with Unit4 Asset Module in March 2026. This system now manages £302.84 million of property, plant and equipment. EY completed audit procedures to verify complete and accurate transfer of data to the new system with no matters to report.
findings.matters: Asset register systems are critical to tracking, valuing, and maintaining control over PPE. Failed implementations can result in material misstatements and loss of asset records. Successful implementation is positive for future asset tracking accuracy and audit efficiency.
findings.figures: £302.84 million of PPE transferred to new system
findings.quote: The Council implemented a new Fixed Asset Register (Unit 4 Asset Module) in March 2026, replacing the previously held manual asset register (Asset 400)... We have completed our work in this area and have no matters to report.

findings.headline: Pension liability valuation work remains incomplete with material differences identified in demographic assumptions following 2025 actuarial valuation.
findings.detail: The audit of pension liabilities is not yet complete. EY's actuarial specialists identified differences outside typical roll-forward tolerance, primarily driven by material demographic assumption updates and experience adjustments following the 2025 triennial valuation. The council's net pension liability is £1.07 million (limited to nil under IFRIC 14) with an additional unfunded liability of £0.116 million.
findings.matters: Pension obligations are material balance sheet liabilities affecting financial position and long-term sustainability. Material changes in demographic assumptions indicate significant changes in the council's long-term commitment to employee benefits and require careful assessment of the impact on financial position.
findings.figures: £1.07 million net liability (limited to nil under IFRIC 14); unfunded liability £0.116 million
findings.quote: A difference outside the specialist's typical roll-forward tolerance was identified in relation to pension liabilities, primarily driven by material demographic assumption updates and experience adjustments following the 2025 valuation. Audit procedures to assess the reasonableness of this difference and confirm that it does not indicate a material misstatement in the year-end liability are currently in progress.

findings.headline: Business rates income for Enterprise Zone properties incorrectly allocated: £0.134 million diverted to general pool instead of designated area income.
findings.detail: Management identified an error in the NNDR3 return where Enterprise Zone properties were misclassified, causing £0.134 million of rates income to be incorrectly allocated to the general business rates pool rather than recognized as designated area income. This was corrected, with consequential correction to creditors and grant income.
findings.matters: Correct allocation of rates income is essential for understanding the council's own-source revenue and impacts on reserves and service delivery funding. Misallocation to the general pool obscures the council's true revenue position from its enterprise zone strategy.
findings.figures: £0.134 million understatement of creditors and overstatement of taxation and non-specific grant income
findings.quote: Management identified an error in the classification of Enterprise Zone properties within the NNDR3 return, resulting in Enterprise Zone rates income being incorrectly allocated to the general business rates pool rather than reported as designated area income. This led to an understatement of creditors and an overstatement of Taxation and Non-Specific Grant Income of £0.134 million.

findings.headline: PWLB loan maturity misclassified: £0.250 million incorrectly recorded in long-term borrowing rather than current borrowings.
findings.detail: During audit testing, EY identified that the current portion of PWLB loans had been classified as long-term borrowing rather than current borrowing. This was corrected by management. The error reflects a tracking issue in the council's debt management processes and affects understanding of near-term refinancing obligations.
findings.matters: Correct classification of debt maturity is essential for lenders to assess refinancing needs, liquidity planning, and debt service obligations over the coming year. Misclassification obscures when loans are due for repayment.
findings.figures: £0.250 million
findings.quote: Reclassification of the current portion of PWLB loans from long-term borrowing to short-term borrowing amounting to £0.250 million.

findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion maintained for 2025/26 with full assurance not anticipated until 2027/28 as part of recovery from 2023/24 disclaimer.
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24 (no assurance possible), qualified in 2024/25, and qualified again in 2025/26. Gaps in assurance persist over comparator income and expenditure balances, property plant and equipment balances, and reserves. An unmodified opinion is anticipated by 2027/28, predominantly due to roll-out of comparator income and expenditure balances.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audit opinions to assess the reliability of financial statements. A qualified opinion indicates ongoing limitations in audit scope that affect confidence in reported balances and the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Disclaimed 2023/24; Qualified 2024/25; Qualified 2025/26; Unqualified anticipated 2027/28
findings.quote: Subject to completion of the remaining outstanding procedures outlined in this report, we expect to issue a qualified (except for) opinion... Gaps in assurance relating to: Comparator income and expenditure balances, property plant and equipment balances and reserves

findings.headline: Additional audit costs beyond scale fee will be incurred to rebuild historical assurance
findings.detail: The risk assessment procedures, work to rebuild assurance over 2022/23 transactions, and the MHCLG capacity submission are outside the scope of the standard scale fee agreed on 29 April 2026. EY will seek a fee variation to cover these incremental costs, but the amount is not yet quantified and will be communicated 'once the costs are agreed'.
findings.matters: Unquantified additional audit costs represent a budget pressure for the council and signal the ongoing scale of remediation work; the absence of a firm figure suggests the scope may still be uncertain.
findings.figures: Scale fee variation to be agreed; quantum not disclosed
findings.quote: Accordingly, we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work and will communicate further through our reporting once the costs are agreed.

findings.headline: Four material reserve categories assessed as higher risk of misstatement, reflecting unaudited balances and weak prior-period controls
findings.detail: EY's risk assessment classified General Fund Balance, Capital Adjustment Account, Revaluation Reserve, and Capital Grants Unapplied Account as presenting higher inherent risk of material misstatement. These assessments reflect large unaudited movements during 2022/23 and 2023/24, the complexity of accounting treatments, reliance on valuation judgements, and susceptibility to management bias in determining available reserves.
findings.matters: Higher-risk reserve classifications indicate that disclosed reserves and financial resilience measures may be unreliable, and that the control environment around these transactions in the disclaimed years remains weak—matters central to creditworthiness and stewardship accountability.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance, Capital Adjustment Account, Revaluation Reserve, Capital Grants Unapplied Account all classified higher risk
findings.quote: The General Fund closing balance is material and represents the cumulative impact of revenue and expenditure decisions over a number of financial periods. Higher inherent risk given the sensitivity of the General Fund balance as a key measure of financial resilience and the potential susceptibility to management bias in determining available usable reserves, with material unaudited movements identified in the disclaimed periods.

findings.headline: £7.8 million of unvalidated property assets will prevent an unqualified opinion until at least 2027
findings.detail: The council operates a rolling 5-year PPE valuation programme. At the end of 2025/26, PPE valued at £7.8 million—last revalued in 2022/23 (the original disclaimed year)—remains unvalidated. EY cannot provide assurance over these assets or their movements through the income statement. The auditor states explicitly that its ability to move to an unqualified opinion depends directly on when this revaluation occurs.
findings.matters: This is a concrete barrier to audit assurance that the council controls through its asset management cycle. The timing is knowable. A lender needs to understand this will be the state of the accounts for at least two more audit years.
findings.figures: £7.8 million PPE, last valued in 2022/23, not revalued by end of 2025/26
findings.quote: At the end of 2025/26 a material value of PPE amounting to £7.8 million last valued in 2022/23, the original disclaimed year, has not been subsequently revalued. We do not have assurance over the valuation of that PPE and associated movements in income and expenditure. Our ability to move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion is therefore dependent on when that PPE is next subject to valuation.

findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion in 2024/25 represents progress from prior disclaimers, but audit assurance gaps remain material
findings.detail: West Suffolk received disclaimed audit opinions in 2022/23 and 2023/24. The 2024/25 audit opinion improved to qualified (except for), indicating partial recovery of assurance. However, the qualification drew attention to remaining areas where sufficient evidence could not be obtained—specifically the valuation of PPE last revalued in 2022/23, and the classification of reserves between usable and unusable categories.
findings.matters: Audit qualifications signal material weaknesses in financial reporting controls and persistent uncertainty over whether the accounts fairly present the council's financial position—the first-order test for any lender or finance director.
findings.figures: 2022/23 (disclaimer), 2023/24 (disclaimer), 2024/25 (qualified except for)
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a qualified audit opinion was issued which drew attention to remaining areas where sufficient appropriate audit evidence was not obtained. These related to the valuation of property, plant and equipment and heritage assets, last revalued in the 2022/23 financial year

findings.headline: Council produced draft accounts one month ahead of extended statutory deadline
findings.detail: West Suffolk signed unaudited 2025-26 accounts on 29 May 2026, one month in advance of the extended deadline of 30 June 2026. The audit opinion is expected well in advance of the 31 January 2027 backstop date.
findings.matters: Early and timely completion of accounts demonstrates effective financial controls and cooperation with auditors. This is a positive signal of council financial management capability.
findings.figures: 29 May 2026, 30 June 2026, 31 January 2027
findings.quote: the council's unaudited 2025 to 2026 Statement of Accounts, signed by the Head of Service (Finance) (Deputy Section 151 Officer) on 29 May 2026 (a month in advance of the extended statutory deadline of 30 June 2026)

findings.headline: External auditor reports no concerns with council's value-for-money arrangements
findings.detail: EY has concluded there are no matters to report on West Suffolk's arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources. This represents a clean value-for-money conclusion separate from the audit opinion qualification.
findings.matters: Value-for-money assessments provide independent verification that the council manages resources effectively and spending is justified. A clean conclusion supports confidence in financial stewardship.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: the auditor has no matters to report on the council's arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in our use of resources

findings.headline: Council's accounts will receive a qualified audit opinion due to opening balance uncertainties from the national local audit backlog
findings.detail: Ernst & Young expects to issue a qualified (except for) opinion for 2025-26, continuing from 2022-23 when the national audit backlog prevented prior-year audits. The qualification stems from insufficient audit work on opening balances in prior years caused by the backlog, not from council performance issues. The auditor explicitly states this occurs 'through no fault of the council'.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial statement reliability through audit opinion status. A qualified opinion affects confidence in reported position, and understanding whether it is systemic or council-specific is material to lending decisions.
findings.quote: The auditors expect to issue a further qualified opinion for the 2025 to 2026 accounts (this practice will continue for multiple audit years through no fault of the council).

findings.headline: Reserves classification can be resolved in the 2025-26 audit, clearing one half of the qualification
findings.detail: Following its risk assessment, EY concluded that it can obtain sufficient assurance over the classification of reserves between usable and unusable categories during the 2025-26 audit, supporting progress toward an unmodified opinion on that issue.
findings.matters: Clearing the reserves qualification demonstrates the council's audit assurance can be rebuilt progressively, restoring lender confidence in reported reserves.
findings.figures: 2025 to 2026 audit
findings.quote: EY have suggested that reserves assurances can be addressed in the 2025 to 2026 audit, supporting progress to a future unmodified opinion.

findings.headline: West Suffolk received disclaimed audit opinions for 2022-23 and 2023-24, then a qualified opinion for 2024-25, all rooted in the national local audit crisis
findings.detail: EY did not audit the 2022-23 accounts due to the nationwide local audit crisis, resulting in disclaimed opinions for both 2022-23 and 2023-24. When audit resumed in 2024-25, a qualified opinion was issued, with the qualification covering PPE valuations and reserve classification.
findings.matters: A string of disclaimed and then qualified audit opinions signals multi-year assurance gaps and material uncertainty over the council's reported financial position.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions 2022-23 and 2023-24; qualified opinion 2024-25
findings.quote: due to the nationwide local audit crisis, EY did not carry out an audit of any 2022 to 2023 accounts. This resulted in disclaimed opinions being issued for West Suffolk's 2022 to 2023 and 2023 to 2024 accounts, and a qualified opinion for the 2024 to 2025 statements.

findings.headline: West Suffolk's audit qualification will remain unresolved until its five-year revaluation programme reaches £7.8 million of property assets, with consequential delays extending two years beyond that point
findings.detail: The council received a qualified audit opinion for 2024-25 relating to property, plant and equipment (PPE) valuations and reserve classifications. While reserves can be addressed in the 2025-26 audit, £7.8 million of assets valued in 2022-23 remain unaudited because they fall outside the current section of the council's five-year revaluation programme. Once these assets are revalued, the impact will take a further two years to flow through the accounts before the qualification can be lifted.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit qualifications indicate areas where auditors lack sufficient assurance, affecting lender confidence in the reliability of the council's reported financial position and reserves.
findings.figures: £7.8 million of assets last valued in 2022 to 2023; two-year lag in accounts impact
findings.quote: at the end of 2025 to 2026 there remained £7.8 million of assets last valued in 2022 to 2023 and, therefore, unaudited. The ability to move forward from a qualified to an unqualified opinion is dependent on when these assets are next subject to a valuation, as the consequential impact on the statements will take a further 2 years to flow through the accounts.

findings.headline: Overall borrowing expected to increase over the year despite early external debt repayment
findings.detail: External borrowing decreased by £125,000 in the first quarter to £8.875m, following the recent £10m PWLB 40-year loan. However, internal borrowing stands at £60.6m and overall borrowing is forecast to increase over the full financial year.
findings.matters: Signals ongoing cash management pressure; the substantial internal borrowing (£60.6m) and expected overall increase warrant monitoring for potential future PWLB drawdown
findings.figures: External borrowing £8,875,000 (down £125,000); internal borrowing £60,634,266
findings.quote: Overall borrowing (total of both external and internal) is expected to increase over the full financial year.

findings.headline: Interest income significantly outperformed budget in the first quarter
findings.detail: The council achieved £341,437 in interest income in the first three months of 2026/27, more than double the budgeted figure of £157,500 for the same period. This represents strong cash management during a period of elevated interest rates.
findings.matters: Material variance to budget indicates either stronger cash generation or more favorable investment rates than forecast; relevant to full-year financial outturn
findings.figures: £341,437 achieved vs £157,500 budgeted (Q1 2026/27)
findings.quote: Interest achieved in the first three months of the financial year amounted to £341,437 against a budget for the period of £157,500.

findings.headline: Capital Projects Financing Reserve of £9.3m provides thin cover against refinancing cost shock
findings.detail: The council has earmarked £9.3m in the Capital Projects Financing Reserve to mitigate adverse interest rate and investment return fluctuations, and specifically to fund additional borrowing costs from PWLB rates higher than assumed in project business cases. The difference between current PWLB rates (6.30%) and budgeted rates creates an annual cost gap that would consume the reserve within ~4.8 years.
findings.matters: The reserve is modest relative to the £57.96m internal borrowing that will eventually require external refinancing. If capital acceleration occurs or rates rise further, the reserve could deplete quickly, leaving no buffer for cost overruns or additional rate rises.
findings.figures: Capital Projects Financing Reserve £9,296,075. Implied annual refinancing cost gap at current rates ~£1.95m (£3,820,756 potential future interest less £1,865,950 budgeted).
findings.quote: The Council has an earmarked revenue reserve to mitigate against possible adverse fluctuations in the returns received from the council's investments and external borrowing costs, called the Capital Projects Financing Reserve. The balance in this reserve as at 31 March 2026 was £9,296,075.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing £57.96m and rising; refinancing to external at 6.30% would add £1.95m annual interest cost
findings.detail: West Suffolk's internal borrowing increased by £8.27m to £57.96m during 2025-26, while external borrowing fell from £9.25m to £9m. The council is funding its capital requirement from cash reserves (now £27.8m, above the £20m forecast) rather than external borrowing. Converting all internal borrowing to 40-year PWLB Certainty Rate borrowing at 6.30% would incur annual interest of £3.82m, versus the budgeted £1.87m—an annual gap of £1.95m.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing relies on available cash; once capital projects spend down reserves, external refinancing becomes mandatory. The rate jump from 1.84% existing to 6.30% new creates a cliff of unexpected additional borrowing costs. This affects debt affordability and could pressure the revenue budget once capital is deployed.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £57,963,592 (up from £49,688,598). Cash held £27,810,000 vs forecast £20,000,000. At 6.30% PWLB Certainty Rate, annual interest on internal borrowing would be £3,820,756 vs budgeted £1,865,950.
findings.quote: if we were to transfer all of that internal borrowing to a 40 year PWLB loan using the 6.30 percent Certainty Rate, the Council would incur an initial annual interest payable cost of £3,820,756 (including our current external borrowing). This compares to our interest payable budget for 2025 to 2026 of £1,865,950.

findings.headline: Capital programme £44.9m underspent, with borrowing requirement only 60% of budget
findings.detail: The council budgeted a £111.9m borrowing requirement to fund capital projects in 2025-26, but actual borrowing requirement at year-end was £66.96m—a £44.9m shortfall (40%). This reflects delayed capital expenditure across major projects including Mildenhall Hub, West Suffolk Operational Hub, Bury Leisure Centre Improvement, and the Net Zero Community Energy Plan. The council's Capital Financing Requirement increased by £8.02m, but was entirely absorbed by internal borrowing from cash reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays create delivery risk on strategic projects and defer revenue cost recognition. More importantly, when projects accelerate and cash depletes, the council will need to externally borrow at PWLB Certainty Rates now at 6.30% for 40-year terms—342 basis points above the 1.84% rate on existing debt.
findings.figures: Budgeted capital borrowing requirement £111,859,015; actual £66,963,592 (variance £44,895,423, 40% underspent).
findings.quote: Borrowing costs only form part of the Councils revenue budget once the project has been completed, so although there may be a borrowing requirement, until such time as the project is complete there will be no MRP or interest payable as part of the revenue budget.

findings.headline: The council is funding the reserve from a one-off Business Rates Equalisation contribution, having previously relied on New Homes Bonus grants which no longer appear available
findings.detail: The only reserve contribution in the forecast period is £2.5m from the Business Rates Equalisation Reserve in 2026/27. The document explicitly states 'The primary source for the funding of this reserve has previously been the New Homes Bonus Grant', indicating a material loss of a previous funding stream. No further contributions of any kind are planned in 2027/28, 2028/29, or 2029/30.
findings.matters: The loss of New Homes Bonus as a source and reliance on a one-off Business Rates contribution signals declining certainty of reserve replenishment. This reinforces that the depletion will be permanent and the council's forward capital funding will depend on borrowing capacity or revenue savings.

findings.matters: Large discretionary capital investments funded from reserves signal the council's growth and regeneration priorities, and indicate it is willing to deplete financial buffers to pursue these objectives. Once reserves are spent, future capital will require borrowing or revenue reduction.

findings.detail: Government grant funding (Revenue Support Grant) falls from £8,220 thousands in 2026-27 to £6,852 thousands in 2028-29, a reduction of £1,368k. The Adjustment Support Grant also phases out entirely by 2029-30. This structural loss of funding is being offset by council tax increases rather than spending reductions.
findings.matters: Declining government funding reduces the proportion of council spending covered by the government, increasing reliance on local taxation and debt, and may indicate a worsening spending/funding gap that cannot be closed by efficiency alone.

findings.matters: Rapidly rising borrowing costs reduce headroom in the revenue budget and are a signal of either planned capital borrowing or refinancing at worse rates; lenders need to understand the source and purpose of this debt.

findings.detail: In the first year alone, the council withdraws £12.732m from earmarked reserves (nearly 27% of the opening balance). Subsequent years see smaller but persistent draws of £1.4-1.5m annually. By 31 March 2030-31, reserves will have declined by £17.1m, reducing the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and may indicate unsustainable spending or use of one-off funding sources rather than sustainable revenue.

findings.detail: The council is projecting balanced budgets for 2026-27 and 2027-28, but the medium-term financial strategy shows 'Remaining budget gap' of (1,243) thousands of pounds in 2028-29 and (3,181) thousands of pounds in 2029-30. findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council has a credible plan to balance its budget and whether deficits will be covered by reserves or further borrowing.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision rising from £1,220k to £2,436k over four years, more than doubling
findings.detail: MRP is forecast to increase from £1,220k in 2025-26 to £1,767k in 2026-27, then £2,357k in 2027-28, and £2,436k in 2028-29. MRP reflects the debt repayment portion of the revenue budget required to cover past and current capital expenditure. This rising profile shows the council will be tied into substantial multi-year debt servicing commitments.
findings.matters: Rising MRP represents an increasing commitment of annual revenue budget to debt repayment, reducing flexibility for service spending. Combined with the rising financing costs indicator, this shows the council faces multi-year pressure on revenue resources.

findings.headline: £56.34m of capital expenditure underspends carried forward from 2025-26 capital budget
findings.detail: The document notes that the stated capital expenditure figures do not include potential capital carry-forward from underspends in the 2025-26 capital budget, currently forecast at £56.34m. This substantial amount is contingent on the S151 Officer's decisions about funding sources and could materially increase future capital programmes and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Large underspends indicate capital delivery challenges or over-programming. When these underspends are spent, they will increase the capital financing requirement and borrowing costs beyond the figures in this plan, amplifying the affordability pressures already flagged by the financing costs spike.
findings.quote: These figures do not include any potential capital expenditure carried forward from underspends in the 2025 to 2026 capital budgets, currently forecast to be £56.34 million.

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow £19.85m in 2026-27 for capital expenditure, with no planned borrowing in the following three years
findings.detail: The capital expenditure financing table shows £19.85m of borrowing funding the 2026-27 capital programme (out of total gross capital expenditure of £40.55m), with nil borrowing in 2027-28 through 2029-30. The concentration of borrowing into a single year drives the spike in financing costs indicators.
findings.matters: The front-loaded borrowing creates multi-year revenue implications through debt servicing costs. A lender would want to understand what capital schemes are driving this £19.85m borrowing and whether the council can sustain the resulting financing costs.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of revenue budget forecast to jump from 4.63% to 15.06% in 2026-27, more than tripling
findings.detail: West Suffolk's prudential indicator for financing costs to net revenue stream shows the proportion of the revenue budget committed to borrowing costs more than tripling from 4.63% forecast in 2025-26 to 15.06% in 2026-27, and continuing to rise to 18.88% in 2027-28. This signals either significantly increased borrowing or material revenue reduction, creating substantial pressure on available resources for service delivery.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the drivers of a three-fold increase in financing costs relative to revenue, and whether the council's borrowing strategy creates unsustainable pressures. For finance directors, this represents a major commitment of revenue budget to debt servicing at a time when councils face spending pressures.

findings.headline: Housing options reserve grows from £2.1m to £3.5m despite overall reserve decline
findings.detail: While total reserves shrink, the housing options reserve is built up deliberately over the plan period. It grows from £2.1m to £3.5m through net contributions averaging £350k per year, with contributions of £1.4–1.6m offset by withdrawals of £1.0–1.3m annually.
findings.matters: Against a backdrop of declining reserves, growth in housing response funding indicates council prioritization of housing pressures. This signals either expected housing demand or a commitment to housing investment, which a lender should understand as a strategic choice.

findings.headline: Total budgeted reserves fall from £47.5m to £30.4m — a 36% decline over four years
findings.detail: Combined reserves drop by £12.7m (27%) in year one alone, from £47.5m to £34.7m, then continue declining to £30.4m by 2029-2030. This represents sustained reserve drawdown with only modest contributions offsetting much larger withdrawals.
findings.matters: Declining reserves over a multi-year period signal structural imbalance between spending and income. Councils unable to maintain or grow reserves over time face reduced financial resilience and may face future constraints on borrowing or service delivery.

findings.headline: Building repairs reserve for leisure facilities depleted to zero by end of 2026-2027 and remains zero throughout the plan
findings.detail: The leisure building repairs reserve of £232k is drawn down completely in year one, with withdrawals (£532k) exceeding opening balance and contributions (£300k). Once empty, annual £300k contributions are matched by equivalent withdrawals, keeping the reserve at zero through 2029-2030.
findings.matters: A zero reserve for leisure building maintenance indicates either completion of works or inability to accumulate buffers for future repairs, reducing the council's flexibility to handle emergency maintenance or asset preservation.
findings.figures: Opening £232,438; 2026-27 withdrawal (£532,438); closing £0 thereafter

findings.headline: Strategic MTFS reserve drawn down by £7.8m in year one, leaving only £415k buffer
findings.detail: The council's main strategic contingency reserve opens at £5.7m but is withdrawn by £7.8m in 2026-2027, with only a £2.5m transfer offsetting the drawdown. The closing balance falls to £415k. This is the thinnest buffer in the four-year plan.
findings.matters: The MTFS reserve is a council's primary contingency for unexpected events or budget pressures. Heavy drawdown in year one of the plan signals the 2026-2027 budget is under strain and depends on using accumulated reserves.

findings.headline: Business rates pool dissolved due to reset risks; council entering new system at baseline with no expected growth.
findings.detail: The business rates system undergoes a complete reset and revaluation in 2026-27. Suffolk's S151 officers decided to exit the pooling arrangement for 2026-27 because of 'risks and uncertainties within the new system'. The council expects to enter at baseline levels and 'do not expect to have significant levels of growth in the first year – indeed there is a risk that one or more pool members may not even achieve baseline levels'.
findings.matters: Business rates are a significant local income source but highly volatile under the new system; the council has no buffer for appeals or revaluation impacts and faces risk of individual authority underperformance affecting the pool.
findings.figures: Tiered levy rates: 10% on 100-110% of baseline, 30% on 110-200%, 45% on 200%+ growth.

findings.headline: Government funding cut in final settlement is offset for 2026-27 only, leaving £1m annual shortfall risk in 2027-28 and 2028-29.
findings.detail: The Final Finance Settlement in February 2026 included a technical correction reducing West Suffolk's funding by £1.2m for 2026-27. Government introduced an Adjustment Support Grant to compensate for that year only. The council assumes this grant continues for 2027-28 and 2028-29 (another £1m each year) but 'there is currently no commitment from the government to continue this support for the other two years'.
findings.matters: If grant ends, the council faces an unplanned £1m shortfall with no identified mitigation in later years; the MTFS assumes continuation without any contingency.
findings.figures: £1.2m reduction in 2026-27, £1.0m in 2027-28 and 2028-29; grant covers 2026-27 only.
findings.quote: There is currently no commitment from the government to continue this support for the other two years of the settlement (2027 to 2029). However, they have stated that they intend to review this.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset in 2026-27 redistributes all accumulated growth; West Suffolk loses benefit of prior years' growth
findings.detail: The new Fair Funding 2.0 settlement includes a full reset of the business rates baseline, meaning all business rates growth accumulated since the scheme began will be redistributed nationally. West Suffolk retains growth only on Enterprise Zones (£400k annually) and Renewable Energy sites (£700k annually), but loses all other accumulated growth. This is a one-time reallocation that helps explain the pressure in the new funding settlement.
findings.matters: Loss of accumulated business rates growth removes a source of discretionary, growth-related funding that councils had relied on for flexibility; this reduces financial resilience and requires offsetting through tax increases or service reductions.
findings.figures: Enterprise Zone growth retained: £400k annually; Renewable Energy growth retained: £700k annually
findings.quote: The business rates retention system will be reset in 2026 to 2027. This means all business rates growth accumulated to date will be redistributed across the sector.

findings.headline: Transitional Protection grant of £1,016k and Recovery Grant of £243k both end after 2028-29, removing support in year the budget gaps emerge
findings.detail: The MTFS discloses two time-limited grants that end after 2028-29. Transitional Protection is worth £1,016k in that year but terminates entirely in 2029-30; the Recovery Grant of £243k also ends. Combined, these represent £1.3m in lost income starting 2029-30. These cliff-edge losses coincide with and exacerbate the structural deficits: the gap worsens from £1.2m in 2028-29 to £3.2m in 2029-30.
findings.matters: Cliff-edge funding losses eliminate predictable income; if a council has not pre-planned savings or alternative income to offset these losses, it faces a funding crisis in the year they terminate.
findings.quote: Transitional Protection will be paid until 2029. The Recovery Grant will be maintained at current levels through to 2029.

findings.headline: West Suffolk is planning £40.55m capital expenditure in 2026-27 funded by £19.85m external borrowing, followed by minimal borrowing thereafter
findings.detail: The capital program is heavily front-loaded: £40.55m in 2026-27 represents 71% of the four-year total, dropping to £5m annually in years 2-4. Of the first-year amount, £19.85m will be financed through unsupported external borrowing at estimated cost of 7% (interest plus minimum revenue provision), with £10.73m from earmarked reserves. No further external borrowing is projected in subsequent years, suggesting a large one-time investment drive.
findings.matters: A large unsecured borrowing commitment (£19-20m) significantly increases debt servicing costs; the council must demonstrate strong business cases and debt sustainability for this scale of issuance, and the cost of this borrowing (£2.3-3.0m annually in Table 1) is already baked into revenue forecasts.
